claim: Each adult abdominal hemisegment (from A1-A7) contains a pair of motoneurons that exit the nerve onto the lateral body wall.
source: Each adult abdominal hemisegment (from A1-A7) contains a pair of motoneurons that exit the nerve onto the lateral body wall (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript describing the anatomical organization of PM-Mns.

claim: In the adult, each motoneuron forms an arborisation that innervates between 15 and 18 parallel muscle fibres that span dorso-ventrally, from the tergites to sternites.
source: In the adult, each motoneuron forms an arborisation that innervates between 15 and 18 parallel muscle fibres that span dorso-ventrally, from the tergites to sternites (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct statement describing the innervation pattern of PM-Mns in adults.

claim: The innervation of the pleural muscles shows variation between segments and between animals.
source: In contrast to the rigid, target-specificity found in the larval neuromuscular system, the innervation of the pleural muscles shows variation between segments and between animals.
evidence: Direct statement comparing PM-Mn innervation to larval neuromuscular system.

claim: Arborisations achieve a consistent spatial organisation with regularly sized, non-overlapping projection fields.
source: Although no one-to-one neuron/muscle targeting is found, arborisations achieve a consistent spatial organisation with regularly sized, non-overlapping projection fields.
evidence: Direct statement describing the spatial organization of PM-Mn arborisations.

claim: By 24 hr APF the majority of larval muscles, and the neurons that innervate them, are removed by programmed cell death and phagocytosis.
source: By 24 hr APF the majority of larval muscles, and the neurons that innervate them, are removed by programmed cell death and phagocytosis (Currie and Bate, 1991).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous work.

claim: At ~24 hr APF axonal regrowth commences with the emergence of filopodia-rich growth cones from the nerve.
source: At ~24 hr APF axonal regrowth commences with the emergence of filopodia-rich growth cones from the nerve.
evidence: Direct statement describing the timing and nature of axonal regrowth.

claim: By 34 hr APF primary branches are established and festooned with filopodia.
source: By 34 hr APF primary branches are established and festooned with filopodia.
evidence: Direct statement describing the developmental stage at 34 hr APF.

claim: The two PM-Mns within each hemisegment segregate into anterior and posterior domains and increase in size and complexity until ~72 hr APF.
source: The two PM-Mns within each hemisegment segregate into anterior and posterior domains and increase in size and complexity until ~72 hr APF.
evidence: Direct statement describing the developmental progression of PM-Mns.

claim: By 84 hr APF the morphology of the arborisations is indistinguishable from that observed at eclosion.
source: By 84 hr APF the morphology of the arborisations is indistinguishable from that observed at eclosion.
evidence: Direct statement describing the maturation of arborisations.

claim: Branch growth is highly dynamic, involving large numbers of filopodia which extend and retract, continually exploring their local environment.
source: Live imaging at 2 min intervals revealed that branch growth is highly dynamic, involving large numbers of filopodia which extend and retract, continually exploring their local environment (Figure 1D).
evidence: Direct statement supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Filopodia are thin (<0.3 µm), motile protrusions with cytoskeletons comprised of parallel F-actin filaments.
source: According to anatomical and molecular criteria, filopodia are considered to be thin (<0.3 µm), motile protrusions with cytoskeletons comprised of parallel F-actin filaments (Mattila and Lappalainen, 2008).
evidence: Definition supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Branches are of higher calibre and less dynamic, with cores containing parallel microtubules and noticeably less F-actin.
source: In contrast, branches are of higher calibre and less dynamic, with cores containing parallel microtubules and noticeably less F-actin.
evidence: Direct statement defining branches in contrast to filopodia.

claim: Lifeact shows enrichment in thin 'filopodia-like' structures.
source: Using Lifeact, a fluorescently tagged F-actin cytoskeletal probe (Riedl et al., 2008), we see enrichment in thin 'filopodia-like' structures (Figure 1E).
evidence: Direct statement supported by imaging data in Figure 1E.

claim: CLIP-170 is found in branches but is mostly excluded from filopodia.
source: In contrast, the plus-end microtubule binding protein CLIP-170 (Stramer et al., 2010), that reveals microtubules, is found in what we refer to as branches but is mostly excluded from filopodia.
evidence: Direct statement describing the localization of CLIP-170.

claim: The majority of filopodia are transient since large numbers are generated and lost between frames.
source: This revealed that that the majority of filopodia are transient since large numbers are generated and lost between frames.
evidence: Direct statement based on time-lapse imaging observations.

claim: A small number of filopodia persist, pioneering individual branches.
source: Despite this, a small number of filopodia persist, pioneering individual branches (white arrowheads).
evidence: Direct statement describing the fate of some filopodia.

claim: Branches also collapse back into single filopodia, highlighting the instability and continuous remodelling of the arborisations at this early stage.
source: In addition, branches also collapse back into single filopodia (yellow arrowhead), highlighting the instability and continuous remodelling of the arborisations at this early stage (see Video 1).
evidence: Direct statement supported by video evidence.

claim: At 35 hr APF neurons and myoblasts are directly apposed to one another.
source: At 35 hr APF neurons and myoblasts are directly apposed to one another (Figure 2A and Video 2).
evidence: Direct statement supported by imaging data.

claim: Growing axonal branches are enveloped by clusters of myoblasts, while more distal growth cones and filopodia extend over sheets of immature myotubes.
source: Growing axonal branches are enveloped by clusters of myoblasts, while more distal growth cones and filopodia extend over sheets of immature myotubes.
evidence: Direct statement describing the spatial relationship between neurons and muscle cells.

claim: 85.1 ± 6.4% of total BRP puncta were localised at branch points and the bases of filopodia.
source: An analysis of BRP::RFP puncta in axon terminals of 5 animals staged from 30 hr to 35 hr APF revealed that 85.1 ± 6.4% (SD) of total BRP puncta were localised at branch points and the bases of filopodia, and 81.6 ± 4.6% of branch points/bases had a punctum (Figure 2C).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of BRP::RFP localization.

claim: 81.6 ± 4.6% of branch points/bases had a BRP punctum.
source: An analysis of BRP::RFP puncta in axon terminals of 5 animals staged from 30 hr to 35 hr APF revealed that 85.1 ± 6.4% (SD) of total BRP puncta were localised at branch points and the bases of filopodia, and 81.6 ± 4.6% of branch points/bases had a punctum (Figure 2C).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of BRP::RFP localization.

claim: BRP::RFP puncta are rapidly recruited to the tips of growing branches where they mark the sites of new filopodia growth.
source: This footage showed that BRP::RFP puncta are rapidly recruited to the tips of growing branches where they mark the sites of new filopodia growth (Figure 2D).
evidence: Direct statement based on time-lapse imaging.

claim: 36.0 ± 12.6% of filopodia emerged from existing BRP puncta.
source: Our analysis found that 36.0 ± 12.6% of filopodia emerged from existing BRP puncta, 48.1 ± 10.7% recruited a punctum within 20 min of their formation and 16.0 ± 11.9% failed to recruit an obvious punctum at all (Figure 2G).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of filopodia and BRP puncta dynamics.

claim: 48.1 ± 10.7% of filopodia recruited a BRP punctum within 20 min of their formation.
source: Our analysis found that 36.0 ± 12.6% of filopodia emerged from existing BRP puncta, 48.1 ± 10.7% recruited a punctum within 20 min of their formation and 16.0 ± 11.9% failed to recruit an obvious punctum at all (Figure 2G).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of filopodia and BRP puncta dynamics.

claim: 16.0 ± 11.9% of filopodia failed to recruit an obvious BRP punctum at all.
source: Our analysis found that 36.0 ± 12.6% of filopodia emerged from existing BRP puncta, 48.1 ± 10.7% recruited a punctum within 20 min of their formation and 16.0 ± 11.9% failed to recruit an obvious punctum at all (Figure 2G).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of filopodia and BRP puncta dynamics.

claim: 100% of filopodia which failed to recruit puncta to their bases were eliminated within 20 min of emergence.
source: In addition, we discovered that 100% of filopodia which failed to recruit puncta to their bases were eliminated within 20 min of emergence (n = 24) (Figure 2H).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of filopodia lifetimes.

claim: The lifetimes of filopodia associated with puncta at their bases were significantly longer than those without.
source: Thus, the lifetimes of filopodia associated with puncta at their bases were significantly longer than those without (Mann- two-tailed Whitney U = 73, p<0.0001) (See Video 3).
evidence: Statistical analysis comparing filopodia lifetimes.

claim: 79.5 ± 3.7% of BRP::RFP puncta in Eve+ interneurons are located at branch points or bases of filopodia.
source: Here we found punctate distributions of BRP::RFP very similar to those in the PM-Mns, with 79.5 ± 3.7% of puncta located at branch points or bases of filopodia (n = 8 output fields from four individuals; Figure 2J and K).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of BRP::RFP localization in interneurons.

claim: At 32 hr APF the PM-Mns are electrically inactive as indicated by the absence of overt changes in GCaMP6m fluorescence.
source: The absence of any overt changes in fluorescence at 32 hr APF indicates that at this stage the motoneurons are electrically inactive.
evidence: Direct statement based on calcium imaging data.

claim: Not until 42 hr APF did we see the first calcium events indicative of membrane depolarisations.
source: Not until 42 hr APF did we see the first calcium events indicative of membrane depolarisations.
evidence: Direct statement based on calcium imaging data.

claim: By 48 hr APF activity was characterised by episodes of transients in quick succession lasting ~8 min, interspersed with longer periods of quiescence.
source: The frequency of calcium events increased sharply and by 48 hr APF activity was characterised by episodes of transients in quick succession lasting ~8 min, interspersed with longer periods of quiescence.
evidence: Direct statement describing calcium activity patterns.

claim: At 74 hr APF bouts of activity contained far greater numbers of events compared to 48 hr APF.
source: Approaching the final stages of arbor growth, at 74 hr APF we observed similar patterns of activity, however now bouts contained far greater numbers of events.
evidence: Direct statement comparing activity at different developmental stages.

claim: Of the eight animals injected with TTX between 24 hr and 32 hr APF, six showed no detectable calcium activity at 78 hr APF.
source: Of the eight animals injected between 24 hr and 32 hr APF, six showed no detectable calcium activity at 78 hr APF (Figure 3B) and two showed only weak transients restricted to small branch segments.
evidence: Direct statement reporting experimental results.

claim: At 79 hr APF the arborisations of animals injected with TTX were morphologically indistinguishable from those injected with buffer.
source: At 79 hr APF we found that the arborisations of animals injected with TTX were morphologically indistinguishable from those injected with buffer (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Direct statement comparing TTX-treated and control arborisations.

claim: Df(2L)VGlut2 completely blocks both evoked and spontaneous glutamatergic neurotransmission.
source: This allele has previously been shown to completely block both evoked and spontaneous glutamatergic neurotransmission (Daniels et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous work.

claim: No significant difference was found between the area of coverage of VGlut null A3-A arborisations and controls.
source: No significant difference was found between the area of coverage of VGlut null A3-A arborisations and controls (Figure 3H), although VGlut nulls were marginally greater in total arbor length (Figure 3I).
evidence: Statistical analysis comparing VGlut null and control arborisations.

claim: VGlut null arborisations were marginally greater in total arbor length compared to controls.
source: No significant difference was found between the area of coverage of VGlut null A3-A arborisations and controls (Figure 3H), although VGlut nulls were marginally greater in total arbor length (Figure 3I).
evidence: Statistical analysis comparing VGlut null and control arborisations.

claim: Before 49 hr APF no calcium events were recorded in the muscles when neurons were stimulated with TRPA1.
source: Before 49 hr APF no calcium events were recorded in the muscles (n = 2; Figure 3J).
evidence: Direct statement reporting experimental results.

claim: Between 50 hr and 59 hr APF a few large calcium events were recorded in the muscles but occurred either during the final seconds of stimulation or just after ramping down the temperature.
source: Between 50 hr and 59 hr APF a few large calcium events were recorded in the muscles but in each case these occurred either during the final seconds of stimulation or just after ramping down the temperature (n = 2).
evidence: Direct statement reporting experimental results.

claim: When stimulating at stages between 68 hr and 72 hr APF we observed robust, rapid and sustained postsynaptic calcium activity.
source: In contrast, when stimulating at stages between 68 hr and 72 hr APF we observed robust, rapid and sustained postsynaptic calcium activity (n = 7; Figure 3J and K).
evidence: Direct statement reporting experimental results.

claim: Between 68–72 hr APF calcium events occurred at significantly greater rates at the permissive temperature (30°C) than at the restrictive temperature (22°C).
source: Between 68–72 hr APF calcium events occurred at significantly greater rates at the permissive temperature (30°C) than at the restrictive temperature (22°C) (6.15 ± 5.60 minute−1 vs 0.93 ± 0.81 minute−1, Mann-Whitney U = 6.0, n = 7, p=0.02, two-tailed).
evidence: Statistical analysis of calcium event rates.

claim: Evoked synaptic transmission does not take place within this system before 60 hr APF.
source: These data indicate that evoked synaptic transmission does not take place within this system before 60 hr APF.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data.

claim: At 34 hr APF, BRP::RFP puncta were found almost exclusively at branch points and at the bases of filopodia.
source: As described previously, at 34 hr APF, BRP::RFP puncta were found almost exclusively at branch points and at the bases of filopodia (white arrowheads).
evidence: Direct statement describing BRP::RFP localization.

claim: By 48 hr APF, in addition to puncta at branch points, many puncta could also be found along the lengths of branches, between branch nodes.
source: By 48 hr APF, in addition to puncta at branch points, many puncta could also be found along the lengths of branches, between branch nodes (yellow arrowheads).
evidence: Direct statement describing changes in BRP::RFP distribution.

claim: At stages 72–77 hr APF, just 12.6 ± 5.8% of BRP::RFP puncta were at branch points, the rest being distributed along branch lengths.
source: Finally, at stages 72–77 hr APF, an analysis of the distribution of puncta revealed that just 12.6 ± 5.8%, n = 5 arborisations from five individuals) of puncta were at branch points, the rest being distributed along branch lengths (Figure 3M).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of BRP::RFP distribution.

claim: 89.4 ± 6.7% of branch points had BRP::RFP puncta at stages 72–77 hr APF.
source: The majority (89.4 ± 6.7%) of branch points however were still found to have puncta.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of BRP::RFP at branch points.

claim: At early stages, BRP::GFP puncta were far more heterogenous in diameter than at later stages.
source: At early stages, puncta were far more heterogenous in diameter than at later stages, measured by a comparison of standard deviations, found to be significant by an F-test of equality of variances (F143,176 = 4.092, p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of BRP::GFP puncta size.

claim: BRP::GFP puncta became significantly smaller over the course of development.
source: We also found that BRP::GFP puncta became significantly smaller over the course of development (Figure 3O).
evidence: Statistical analysis of BRP::GFP puncta size over time.

claim: No detectable GluRIIE was evident at 48 hr APF.
source: No detectable GluRIIE was evident at 48 hr APF (Figure 3P) yet by 85 hr APF clear clusters of GluRIIE were found apposed to the branches (Figure 3Q).
evidence: Direct statement based on imaging data.

claim: By 85 hr APF clear clusters of GluRIIE were found apposed to the branches.
source: No detectable GluRIIE was evident at 48 hr APF (Figure 3P) yet by 85 hr APF clear clusters of GluRIIE were found apposed to the branches (Figure 3Q).
evidence: Direct statement based on imaging data.

claim: Both Nlg1 and Nrx nulls show comparable defects in arbor morphology, with large reductions in coverage relative to wild-type controls.
source: At late pupal stages we found that both Nlg1 and Nrx nulls show comparable defects in arbor morphology, with large reductions in coverage relative to wild-type controls (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Direct statement comparing mutant and control phenotypes.

claim: Nlg1 and Nrx null arborisations showed significant reductions in area of coverage and total arbor length compared to wild-type controls.
source: Nlg1 and Nrx null arborisations showed significant reductions in area of coverage and total arbor length compared to wild-type controls (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Statistical analysis comparing mutant and control arborisations.

claim: No differences were found between total branch numbers in Nlg1 nulls, Nrx nulls, and controls.
source: We found no differences between total branch numbers (Figure 4E).
evidence: Statistical analysis comparing branch numbers.

claim: Nrx and Nlg1 null arborisations did not differ significantly from each other in any of these measurements.
source: Nrx and Nlg1 null arborisations did not differ significantly from each other in any of these measurements.
evidence: Statistical comparison between mutant phenotypes.

claim: Nlg1 and Nrx null arborisations did not differ significantly from controls in the maximum number of branch orders.
source: With this we found no differences in the maximum number of branch orders.
evidence: Statistical analysis using Strahler method.

claim: The total number of lowest order (terminal) branches did not differ significantly between Nlg1 nulls, Nrx nulls, and controls.
source: Furthermore, the total number of lowest order (terminal) branches did not differ significantly between the groups; a trend which continued for subsequent orders, with all conditions having remarkably similar numbers of branches at every level.
evidence: Statistical analysis of branch ordering.

claim: Nlg1 null branches were significantly less straight than those of the controls at stages between 30 hr and 36 hr APF.
source: Nlg1 null branches were found to be significantly less straight than those of the controls (Mann-Whitney U = 441, p<0.0001, two-tailed).
evidence: Statistical analysis of branch bendiness.

claim: Complete induction of Nlg1 D-lock (disrupting) clones produces arbor growth defects comparable to Nlg1 mutants.
source: These displayed a very similar arbor growth phenotype to Nlg1 nulls (Figure 5D).
evidence: Direct statement comparing FlpStop disruption to null mutants.

claim: Germline ND-lock rescues arbor growth to a near wild-type phenotype.
source: In this case, arbor growth was rescued to a near wild-type phenotype (Figure 5E).
evidence: Direct statement describing rescue experiment results.

claim: Branches growing across ND-lock clonal myotubes, in which Nlg1 expression was rescued, displayed more wild-type-like morphologies than those growing on non-clonal fibres.
source: Using the allele in the initially disrupting orientation the reverse situation was observed; branches growing across ND-lock clonal myotubes, in which Nlg1 expression was rescued, displayed more wild-type-like morphologies than those growing on non-clonal fibres (n = 7 muscle mosaics; Figure 5I).
evidence: Direct statement describing mosaic analysis results.

claim: At 35 hr APF Nlg1::GFP faintly labels the entire postsynaptic membrane, but forms strong puncta only at sites that directly appose the axon terminals.
source: At 35 hr APF Nlg1::GFP faintly labels the entire postsynaptic membrane, but forms strong puncta only at sites that directly appose the axon terminals (Figure 6A).
evidence: Direct statement based on imaging data.

claim: Nlg1::GFP puncta are concentrated on growing axonal branches, particularly at branch points and at the very tips of exploratory filopodia.
source: Higher magnifications showed a concentration of puncta on growing axonal branches, particularly at branch points and at the very tips of exploratory filopodia (Figure 6B and Video 7).
evidence: Direct statement based on high magnification imaging.

claim: Nlg1::GFP puncta are recruited directly onto filopodia and at the tips of branches.
source: In this footage we found that Nlg1::GFP puncta are recruited directly onto filopodia and at the tips of branches.
evidence: Direct statement based on time-lapse imaging.

claim: Branch growth occurs as a highly coordinated sequence where the arrival of Nlg1::GFP on exploratory processes precedes their stabilisation and maturation into stable branches in an iterative manner.
source: As a result, branch growth occurs as a highly coordinated sequence where the arrival of Nlg1::GFP on exploratory processes precedes their stabilisation and maturation into stable branches in an iterative manner.
evidence: Direct statement describing the temporal relationship between Nlg1::GFP and branch growth.

claim: Nlg1::GFP puncta apposed to growth cones and filopodia were often found to be stable for many minutes.
source: Nlg1::GFP puncta in apposition to growth cones and filopodia were often found to be stable for many minutes.
evidence: Direct statement based on time-lapse imaging.

claim: Nlg1::GFP puncta apposed to filopodia appeared to correlate with filopodia longevity.
source: Furthermore, puncta apposed to filopodia appeared to correlate with filopodia longevity (white arrowheads), and regularly marked the limits of filopodial retraction (yellow arrowhead).
evidence: Direct statement based on time-lapse imaging observations.

claim: Filopodia tipped by Nlg1::GFP puncta were significantly longer lived than filopodia not bearing puncta.
source: Thus, filopodia tipped by Nlg1::GFP puncta were significantly longer lived than filopodia not bearing puncta (Figure 6E).
evidence: Statistical analysis of filopodia lifetimes.

claim: Nrx::GFP has a punctate distribution in growing branches, particularly at points of filipodia growth and at filopodial tips, much like Nlg1::GFP.
source: Using GFP tagged Nrx1 (hereon termed Nrx) (Banovic et al., 2010) expressed in motoneurons we observed a punctate distribution in growing branches, particularly at points of filipodia growth and at filopodial tips, much like Nlg1::GFP (Figure 6F and Video 8).
evidence: Direct statement comparing Nrx::GFP and Nlg1::GFP localization.

claim: Liprin-α::GFP forms distinct puncta at branch terminals and within filopodia.
source: Much like Nrx::GFP, Liprin-α::GFP forms distinct puncta at branch terminals and within filopodia (Figure 7A).
evidence: Direct statement based on imaging data.

claim: Presynaptic Liprin-α::GFP puncta often mark the limits of filopodial retraction.
source: Similarly to postsynaptic Nlg1::GFP, we found that presynaptic Liprin-α::GFP puncta often mark the limits of filopodial retraction (Figure 7B) and appeared to correlate with filopodial stability (see Video 9).
evidence: Direct statement based on time-lapse imaging.

claim: Filopodia bearing Liprin-α::GFP puncta were significantly longer lived than those not.
source: Indeed, filopodia bearing Liprinα::GFP puncta were significantly longer lived than those not (Figure 7C).
evidence: Statistical analysis of filopodia lifetimes.

claim: Liprin-α::GFP coalesces into puncta directly on filopodia.
source: It appears that Liprin-α::GFP coalesces into puncta directly on filopodia (Figure 7D).
evidence: Direct statement based on time-lapse imaging.

claim: The large majority of Liprin-α::GFP and Syd1::Straw puncta were coincident, including those at the tips of filopodia.
source: The large majority of puncta of each protein were coincident, including those at the tips of filopodia (Figure 7E).
evidence: Direct statement based on dual-label imaging.

claim: When Liprin-α::GFP and BRP::RFP were expressed together there was very little co-localisation at branch points and never at filopodia tips.
source: In contrast, when Liprin-α::GFP and BRP::RFP were expressed together there was very little co-localisation at branch points and never at filopodia tips (Figure 7F).
evidence: Direct statement based on dual-label imaging.

claim: Without Nlg1, Liprin-α::GFP puncta are largely absent from the unusually long and unbranched terminal branches, typical of growing Nlg1 null arborisations.
source: On closer inspection however, we found that Liprin-α::GFP puncta are largely absent from the unusually long and unbranched terminal branches, typical of growing Nlg1 null arborisations (white arrowheads).
evidence: Direct statement based on imaging of Nlg1 null mutants.

claim: Unusually long and unbranched terminal branches in Nlg1 nulls invariably collapse back or fail to grow any further.
source: When followed, these branches invariably collapse back or fail to grow any further (n = 4 arborisations from four individuals), resulting in the characteristically stunted appearance of Nlg1 null arborisations.
evidence: Direct statement based on time-lapse imaging of Nlg1 nulls.

claim: Liprin-α::GFP is localised to the tips and along the lengths of filopodia on the growing axonal output arborisations of Eve+ interneurons.
source: Like in growing axon terminals of PM-Mn neurons, Liprin-α::GFP is localised to the tips and along the lengths of filopodia on the growing axonal output arborisations (Figure 7I).
evidence: Direct statement based on imaging of interneurons.

claim: Elevated postsynaptic Nlg1 levels resulted in compacted axon terminals at 33–35 hr APF, with distal branches transformed into flattened growth cones with many filopodia.
source: Elevated postsynaptic Nlg1 levels resulted in compacted axon terminals at 33–35 hr APF, with distal branches transformed into flattened growth cones with many filopodia (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: Direct statement describing gain-of-function phenotype.

claim: Elevated postsynaptic Nlg1 levels led to late stage arborisations with reduced branch length, territory and complexity.
source: This significant effect on growth led to late stage arborisations with reduced branch length, territory and complexity (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: Direct statement describing gain-of-function phenotype.

claim: At 35 hr APF, PM-Mn motoneuron branches show preferential elaboration onto clonal Nlg1untagged expressing myotubes and myoblast clusters.
source: At early stages (35 hr APF), PM-Mn growth appeared to be directed onto myoblast clusters/developing myotubes that strongly expressed the Nlg1untagged (Figure 8F).
evidence: Direct statement based on mosaic analysis.

claim: By later stages (70 hr APF), branches in contact with strongly expressing clonal fibres displayed the same hyper-stabilisation phenotype seen with full muscle expression.
source: By later stages (70 hr APF), branches in contact with these strongly expressing clonal fibres displayed the same hyper-stabilisation phenotype seen with full muscle expression.
evidence: Direct statement based on mosaic analysis.

claim: Branches from the same neuron in contact with low to non-expressing fibres grew as normal.
source: In contrast, branches from the same neuron in contact with low to non-expressing fibres grew as normal, demonstrating unequivocally that Nlg1 impacts branch growth via local mechanisms (Figure 8G).
evidence: Direct statement based on mosaic analysis.

claim: When v'ada was made to misexpress Nlg1untagged, PM-Mn axon branches grow perpendicular to the normal arborisation between muscle fibres to contact v'ada sensory neurites.
source: In contrast, when v'ada was made to misexpress Nlg1untagged, PM-Mn axon branches grow perpendicular to the normal arborisation between muscle fibres to contact v'ada sensory neurites (Figure 8L–N).
evidence: Direct statement describing ectopic expression experiment.

claim: Conspicuous concentrations of BRP were found at each contact between PM-Mn axon branches and v'ada dendrites expressing Nlg1untagged.
source: As shown in Figure 8O, conspicuous concentrations of BRP were found at each contact.
evidence: Direct statement based on immunohistochemistry.

claim: The density of synapses was not significantly different between Nlg1 or Nrx nulls and wild-type controls.
source: We found that the density of synapses was not significantly different between Nlg1 or Nrx nulls and wild-type controls, although it was slightly higher in Nlg1 gain-of-function animals (Figure 9B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of synapse density.

claim: Synapse density was slightly higher in Nlg1 gain-of-function animals compared to controls.
source: We found that the density of synapses was not significantly different between Nlg1 or Nrx nulls and wild-type controls, although it was slightly higher in Nlg1 gain-of-function animals (Figure 9B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of synapse density.

claim: In wild-type controls, muscle calcium events at late pupal/pharate stages usually occur in synchrony across the muscle field.
source: In wild-type controls, muscle calcium events at this stage usually occur in synchrony across the muscle field (Figure 9C and D and Video 10).
evidence: Direct statement based on calcium imaging.

claim: In Nlg1 gain-of-function pupae, calcium events were more common in some groups of fibres than others, resulting in far less synchronicity.
source: In contrast, in Nlg1 gain-of-function pupae, calcium events were more common in some groups of fibres than others, resulting in far less synchronicity (Figure 9E and F and Video 11).
evidence: Direct statement based on calcium imaging.

claim: The climbing speed of Nlg1 nulls was significantly lower than controls.
source: Using videography and an automated tracking software we found that the climbing speed of Nlg1 nulls (n = 11) was significantly lower than controls (n = 10) (t(8.15) = 19, p<0.0001, t-test, two-tailed) (Figure 9H).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Disruptions to leg motoneuron axon terminals were found in Nlg1 nulls.
source: We found disruptions to leg motoneuron axon terminals in Nlg1 nulls, suggesting that some of this deficit may be a direct result of abnormal innervation at the neuromusclar junction(Figure 9I).
evidence: Direct statement based on imaging data.

claim: PM-Mn axonal arborisations grow exuberantly, by trial-and-error, very much like complex neurons found in vertebrate central nervous systems.
source: Also, unlike larval motoneuron terminals, which grow incrementally to scale with the changes in muscle size during larval life, the PM-Mn axonal arborisations grow exuberantly, by trial-and-error, very much like complex neurons found in vertebrate central nervous systems.
evidence: Direct comparison to vertebrate neurons.

claim: Branch growth is driven by dynamic complexes formed between synaptic partners that we term 'neuritic adhesion complexes' (NACs).
source: Importantly, we find that branch growth is driven by dynamic complexes formed between synaptic partners that we term 'neuritic adhesion complexes' (NACs).
evidence: Direct statement introducing the NAC concept.

claim: NACs contain Nlg1 (postsynaptically), along with Nrx, Syd1 and Liprin-α (presynaptically).
source: These NACs contain Nlg1 (postsynaptically), along with Nrx, Syd1 and Liprin-α (presynaptically), and act locally to stabilise filopodia by a 'stick and grow' mechanism without the need of synaptic vesicle release machinery or functional synapses.
evidence: Direct statement describing NAC composition.

claim: NACs act locally to stabilise filopodia by a 'stick and grow' mechanism without the need of synaptic vesicle release machinery or functional synapses.
source: These NACs contain Nlg1 (postsynaptically), along with Nrx, Syd1 and Liprin-α (presynaptically), and act locally to stabilise filopodia by a 'stick and grow' mechanism without the need of synaptic vesicle release machinery or functional synapses.
evidence: Direct statement describing NAC function.

claim: Knockdowns of either evoked or spontaneous neurotransmission do not impact arbor growth.
source: Knockdowns of either evoked or spontaneous neurotransmission do not impact arbor growth.
evidence: Direct statement from the abstract summarizing experimental findings.

claim: Axonal branch growth is regulated by dynamic, focal localisations of Neurexin and Neuroligin.
source: Instead, we find that axonal branch growth is regulated by dynamic, focal localisations of Neurexin and Neuroligin.
evidence: Direct statement from the abstract summarizing findings.

claim: These adhesion complexes provide stability for filopodia by a 'stick-and-grow' based mechanism wholly independent of synaptic activity.
source: These adhesion complexes provide stability for filopodia by a 'stick-and-grow' based mechanism wholly independent of synaptic activity.
evidence: Direct statement from the abstract summarizing the mechanism.

claim: These accumulations of presynaptic proteins do not appear to be presynaptic release sites and are not paired with neurotransmitter receptors.
source: These accumulations of presynaptic proteins do not appear to be presynaptic release sites and are not paired with neurotransmitter receptors.
evidence: Direct statement from the abstract summarizing findings.

claim: The synaptotropic hypothesis posits that the stability of growing axonal and dendritic branches is controlled by the selective stabilisation of processes by nascent synapses.
source: The synaptotropic hypothesis posits that the stability of growing axonal and dendritic branches is controlled by the selective stabilisation of processes by nascent synapses, encouraging growth into territories rich in potential synaptic partners.
evidence: Statement describing a hypothesis from the literature.

claim: Live imaging in vertebrate brains has revealed dynamic axonal and dendritic growth where the arrival and localisation of synaptic machineries is correlated with branch stabilisation.
source: Since then, live imaging in vertebrate brains has revealed dynamic axonal and dendritic growth (Kaethner and Stuermer, 1992; Wu et al., 1999; Jontes et al., 2000; Hossain et al., 2012) where the arrival and localisation of synaptic machineries is correlated with branch stabilisation (Alsina et al., 2001; Niell et al., 2004; Meyer and Smith, 2006; Ruthazer et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Data on Xenopus tectal neuron dendritic growth revealed a role for Neurexin (Nrx) and Neuroligin (Nlg) in branch dynamics, whereby Nrx-Nlg interactions are believed to direct the genesis and maturation of opposing hemisynapses, after which neurotransmission stabilises branches.
source: Data on Xenopus tectal neuron dendritic growth revealed a role for Neurexin (Nrx) and Neuroligin (Nlg) in branch dynamics, whereby Nrx-Nlg interactions are believed to direct the genesis and maturation of opposing hemisynapses, after which neurotransmission stabilises branches (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: The idea that synaptic transmission stabilises nascent contacts during elaboration is supported by a number of studies.
source: The idea that synaptic transmission stabilises nascent contacts during elaboration is supported by a number of studies (Rajan et al., 1999; Sin et al., 2002; Ruthazer et al., 2003; Haas et al., 2006; Ruthazer et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Other work has suggested that activity has little impact on large-scale features of tree growth but plays a more nuanced role in refining structural connectivity during activity dependent plasticity.
source: However, other work has suggested that activity has little impact on large-scale features of tree growth but plays a more nuanced role in refining structural connectivity during activity dependent plasticity (Verhage et al., 2000; Varoqueaux et al., 2002; Hua et al., 2005; Ben Fredj et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Liprin-α is a scaffolding protein that is one of the first components recruited to trans-synaptic Nrx-Nlg1 complexes.
source: Liprin-α (Lar interacting protein) is a scaffolding protein that is one of the first components recruited to trans-synaptic Nrx-Nlg1 complexes (Owald et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: The early accumulations of presynaptic proteins seen in early arborisations (i.e. 30–40 hr APF) may mark stable sites or 'transport hubs' that help store/sort synaptic proteins for a later role in synapse formation.
source: The accumulations of presynaptic proteins seen in early arborisations (i.e. 30–40 hr APF) may instead mark stable sites or 'transport hubs' that help store/sort synaptic proteins for a later role in synapse formation.
evidence: Speculative statement about the function of presynaptic protein accumulations.

claim: Syd-1 and Liprin-α have been found to play a key role in orchestrating synapse assembly by recruiting and retaining other synaptic proteins.
source: Previously, Syd-1 and Liprin-α have been found to play a key role in orchestrating synapse assembly by recruiting and retaining other synaptic proteins.
evidence: Statement about known functions of Syd-1 and Liprin-α.

claim: Liprin-α, Syd-1 and Nrx puncta at early stages of exuberant growth are transient and do not appear to become 'future synapses'.
source: Liprin-α, Syd-1 and Nrx puncta at these stages of exuberant growth are transient and do not appear to become 'future synapses'.
evidence: Direct statement based on observations.

claim: The fluidity of Liprin-α, Syd-1 and Nrx puncta speaks to a role in branch morphogenesis rather than in a stepwise, clockwork assembly of synaptic machinery at a particular place.
source: Their fluidity speaks to a role in branch morphogenesis rather than in a stepwise, clockwork assembly of synaptic machinery at a particular place.
evidence: Inference based on observed dynamics.

claim: Dynamic interactions between filopodia and the postsynaptic target are fundamental determinants of tree construction.
source: That we see direct evidence for the formation of these NACs on filopodia themselves suggests that dynamic interactions between filopodia and the postsynaptic target are fundamental determinants of tree construction.
evidence: Inference based on observations of NAC formation.

claim: Mice lacking three Nlg homologues or all three α-Nrxs build brains with grossly normal cytoarchitectures and synapse densities.
source: Others have shown that mice lacking three Nlg homologues or all three α-Nrxs build brains with grossly normal cytoarchitectures and synapse densities (Missler et al., 2003; Varoqueaux et al., 2006) and posit that their role is solely to modulate synapse function.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Disrupting Nlg1/Nrx signalling ultimately has little effect on the timing of synapse development and size of active zones.
source: In addition, we find that disrupting Nlg1/Nrx signalling ultimately has little effect on the timing of synapse development and size of active zones, suggesting that tree morphogenesis is uncoupled from the formation of synapses.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing findings.

claim: Tree morphogenesis is uncoupled from the formation of synapses.
source: In addition, we find that disrupting Nlg1/Nrx signalling ultimately has little effect on the timing of synapse development and size of active zones, suggesting that tree morphogenesis is uncoupled from the formation of synapses.
evidence: Inference based on experimental findings.

claim: Disruptions in functional connectivity could largely be due to disruptions in growth and morphology of the arborisation.
source: One prediction from this is that disruptions in functional connectivity could largely be due to disruptions in growth and morphology of the arborisation.
evidence: Prediction based on findings.

claim: Ectopically expressing Nlg1 in class IV da sensory neurons results in the generation of a 'synthetic connectivity' on the normally 'asynaptic' da sensory neurites, with the development of mature, differentiated presynaptic structures in later pupal stages.
source: An important observation that frames this is the outcome of ectopically expressing Nlg1 in class IV da sensory neurons. There we see the generation of a 'synthetic connectivity' on the normally 'asynaptic' da sensory neurites, with the development of mature, differentiated presynaptic structures in later pupal stages i.e. sites marked by BRP and synaptic vesicle proteins.
evidence: Direct statement describing experimental results.

claim: The normal patterns of muscle activity are disrupted when Nlg1 is overexpressed, with changes in the frequency and spatial heterogeneity of calcium events.
source: In support of this, our calcium imaging reveals that the normal patterns of muscle activity are disrupted when Nlg1 is overexpressed, with changes in the frequency and spatial heterogeneity of calcium events.
evidence: Direct statement based on calcium imaging data.

claim: Elevated postsynaptic Nlg1 expression results in irregular innervation.
source: Since elevated postsynaptic Nlg1 expression results in condensed arborisations, we propose that this is a result of irregular innervation.
evidence: Inference based on morphological observations.

claim: Nlg1 null adults had significant motor behaviour deficits.
source: The behavioural analysis shows that Nlg1 null adults had significant motor behaviour deficits.
evidence: Direct statement based on behavioral analysis.

claim: These data provide a link between an adhesion-based mechanism of arbor growth and synaptic connectivity, which ultimately affects function.
source: Taken together these data provide a link between an adhesion-based mechanism of arbor growth and synaptic connectivity, which ultimately affects function.
evidence: Summary statement linking findings.

claim: In growing arborisations we see branch dynamics and localisations of presynaptic proteins very similar to the 'synaptotropic growth' described in fish/frogs.
source: In growing arborisations we see branch dynamics and localisations of presynaptic proteins very similar to the 'synaptotropic growth' described in fish/frogs.
evidence: Direct statement from the abstract comparing findings to vertebrate systems.

claim: This early role for Nlg1/Nrx based NACs in arbor growth is supported by strong evidence that exploratory filopodia and branch tips are highly sensitive to changes in the early expression of postsynaptic Nlg1.
source: This early role for Nlg1/Nrx based NACs in arbor growth is supported by strong evidence that exploratory filopodia and branch tips are highly sensitive to changes in the early expression of postsynaptic Nlg1.
evidence: Summary statement linking observations.

claim: There is some indication of preferential growth into regions with elevated postsynaptic Nlg1 expression.
source: Moreover there is some indication of preferential growth into regions with elevated postsynaptic Nlg1 expression.
evidence: Statement based on mosaic analysis observations.

claim: Wildtype PM-Mns grow past muscles, into novel territories and make contacts with class IV da sensory neurons ectopically expressing Nlg1.
source: We were very surprised to see wildtype PM-Mns grow past muscles, into novel territories and make contacts with class IV da sensory neurons ectopically expressing Nlg1.
evidence: Direct statement describing experimental results.
